extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and intermediate fiction writers (students of Gotham Writers' Workshop)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for writing fiction (short stories, novellas, novels) covering idea generation, characterization, plot, point of view, scenecraft, description, dialogue, voice, revision, and the business of publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Fiction is a made-up story told in prose with words alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the unique challenge of creating immersive reality using only language; aim to engage the reader's imagination so they 'step through the looking-glass.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Form: novel, novella, short story
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose the appropriate form—novel (roughly 80k+ words), novella (15k–80k), or short story (typically ≤15k, often much shorter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let the story determine its form: novels allow breadth and many elements, short stories require precision and economy ('every word counts'), novellas sit between. Don't force a story into the wrong form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary vs. genre fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish literary fiction (aspiring to art/depth) from genre fiction (mystery, thriller, sci‑fi, romance, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both are valid and share craft fundamentals; literary should still entertain, genre benefits from insight and resonance. Teachings in the book focus mostly on literary fiction, but core craft applies to all genres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idea generation (seeds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Find story seeds everywhere—personal life, newspapers, history, overheard dialogue, objects, feelings, names, structures, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep a notebook; write down many possible seeds and pick the one that 'gives you a buzz.' Remember a seed is only a beginning—cultivate many connected ideas to grow a full story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write daily / show up for work
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing is a craft improved by practice—regular, persistent writing rather than waiting for genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice frequently; prioritize motivation and work ethic over imaginary instant brilliance. Use exercises in the book to build habit and output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transform fact into fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Use real-life events as inspiration but fictionalize them—shape, compress, and alter facts to make a better story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid slavish adherence to literal facts which can create flat or indulgent narratives; bend reality to heighten shape, suspense, clarity, irony, and emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show vs. tell
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer dramatic, sensory scenes ('show') over exposition and summary ('tell'), which distance readers from experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scenes to enact action and emotional transformation; reserve telling for necessary transitions, condensation, or when summary better serves pacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: desire/goal (motivation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should have clear desires or goals that drive action and plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong protagonist's desire forms the engine of plot and the 'major dramatic question.' Use desire to generate conflict, choices, and consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character complexity and change
rubrics_metrics.description: Create characters with depth (contradictory traits, interior life) who are capable of change over the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid flat or purely archetypal figures; show inner contradictions, growth or failure, and evidence of history and drives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain believable behavior and development—characters must act in ways consistent with their established traits and circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inconsistencies should be motivated and earned; keep track of character history and the 'POV contract' to avoid jarring shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of revealing character
rubrics_metrics.description: Reveal characters through actions, dialogue, appearance, thoughts, choices, and how others respond to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer showing through behavior and specific detail rather than blunt authorial description; use 'telling details' smartly to indicate nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character appearance and relevant detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Select specific, telling physical and behavioral details that reveal character and support scene focus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid exhaustive physical catalogs; choose details that illuminate personality or history and serve the scene's needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Names
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose character names thoughtfully to fit tone, period, and characterization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Names can carry subtext or clash deliberately; ensure they serve the story and don't distract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot structure (beginning, middle, end)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize plot with a clear beginning that sets up the major dramatic question, a middle where conflict intensifies, and an end with consequences and resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use structure to maintain focus; beginnings should hook and orient, middles should complicate and develop stakes, ends should pay off the dramatic question rather than rely on deus ex machina.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major dramatic question
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the central question the story asks (e.g., will X achieve Y?).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep this question alive as the guiding plot thread; it clarifies stakes and shapes readers' expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict and stakes
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce meaningful conflict that creates obstacles to characters' desires; escalate stakes toward crisis and climax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make consequences matter; small, intimate stakes can be powerful if emotionally charged; avoid solutions that feel unearned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene vs. summary
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish scene (dramatic enactment in present tense/narrative time) from summary (condensed narration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scenes to show turning points and character interaction; use summary for necessary compression, transitions, or less-important stretches of time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Control the story's tempo through scene length, sentence rhythm, paragraphing, and distribution of action and reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust pace to fit mood and plot: speed up during action, slow for reflection; vary rhythm to maintain reader interest and manage exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting: place, time, mood
rubrics_metrics.description: Use setting to anchor scenes (place, time, atmosphere) and to interact with character and plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe setting with specific, sensory details that affect character behavior or mood; avoid decorative description that doesn't serve story needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description: sensory and specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe via sensory detail (sight, sound, smell, touch, taste) and precise, specific images rather than vague generalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer telling details that evoke a larger truth; specificity grounds reader and makes scenes believable and memorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telling details vs. clichés
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose original, telling details rather than clichéd or generic images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Telling details should feel fresh and surprising while revealing character or theme; avoid overused metaphors and stock descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figurative language (metaphor, simile, synesthesia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use figurative language to illuminate and enrich, but sparingly and purposefully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figurative language should clarify experience or create resonance; avoid mixed metaphors, pretentious flourishes, or gratuitous ornamentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice: finding and consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop a distinctive narrative voice (conversational, formal, ceremonial, natural, etc.) and maintain its consistency throughout the piece.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voice affects diction, sentence rhythm, and point of view; ensure voice fits the narrator and genre and does not shift without reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view (POV) and POV contract
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose an appropriate POV (first-person variations, third-person single/multiple/omniscient, second-person) and honor the implicit 'contract' with reader about what the narrator can know or report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be consistent about narrative distance and limits; violations of POV (head-hopping, unjustified omniscience) break reader trust. Choose POV that best serves intimacy and scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-person variations
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand first-person types: reliable/unreliable, peripheral, multiple vision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use unreliability deliberately; peripheral narrators can reveal other characters indirectly; ensure voice, credibility, and limitations are coherent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-person variations
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish third-person single vision, multiple vision, objective, and omniscient narration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Third-person single keeps close to one character's perspective; omniscient must be controlled and purposeful; multiple vision requires clear transitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distance in POV (emotional & time)
rubrics_metrics.description: Control how close the narrative is emotionally and temporally to events (immediacy vs. reflective distance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distance affects reader empathy and tone; choose close immediacy for visceral scenes and reflective distance for theme or commentary, but remain consistent where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue: realism and conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Write dialogue that sounds real, reveals character, and advances plot while observing readable conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid writing exact speech verbatim; use subtext, stage directions sparingly, and balance dialogue with beats and tags. Dialogue should feel natural yet focused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue tags and beats
rubrics_metrics.description: Use tags ('he said') and beats (physical actions) to attribute speech and add texture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer simple tags like 'said' for invisibility; use action beats to reveal character and avoid overuse of adverbial tags.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtext in dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Convey underlying meanings and emotions through subtext rather than explicit statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let what characters do and how they speak imply motives and conflicts; subtext enriches scenes and avoids didactic chatter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect dialogue and summary
rubrics_metrics.description: Use indirect discourse to summarize conversations or to report speech without full dramatization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use indirect dialogue when the content matters more than the moment-to-moment enactment, or to manage pacing and compression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialect and profanity
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent dialect and colloquial speech with care to capture voice without alienating readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dialect sparingly and consistently; focus on rhythm and selective markers rather than attempting full-phonetic transcription; use profanity purposefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theme: definition and emergence
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop a theme (what the story is about beyond plot) that emerges organically from character, action, and pattern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't preach; let theme affect choices of detail, repetition, and consequence. Sleuth out theme by revising and noting recurring motifs and tensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theme affects everything
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure theme subtly influences character behavior, imagery, structure, and ending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When theme informs craft choices, the story gains resonance. Revision can reveal and refine thematic threads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision: process and drafts
rubrics_metrics.description: Revision is essential—produce drafts, then re-envision, restructure, and rewrite at macro and micro levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stages include first draft creation, prelude to revision (detachment), big-picture reenvisioning, then microrevision (sentence-level). Allow time and distance before revising; read aloud and get feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision: big things vs. little things
rubrics_metrics.description: Address big structural problems (plot, POV, character arcs, theme) before micro-editing (word choice, syntax, punctuation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid polishing sentences until the story's architecture and emotional logic are secure; use cutting and expansion where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Microrevision and tweaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Fine-tune sentences, paragraphs, rhythm, diction, and punctuation to sharpen voice and clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work on verbs and nouns, eliminate pretentious or unnecessary words (especially adverbs), and attend to sentence variety and flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cutting
rubrics_metrics.description: Be ruthless in cutting extraneous material that doesn't serve story focus, tension, or character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short fiction especially demands strict economy; remove scenes, lines, or details that dilute the central effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading aloud and distance for editing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use reading aloud and stepping away from the manuscript to gain perspective when revising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading aloud reveals rhythm issues and clumsy phrasing; distance helps spot structural problems and emotional redundancies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence, paragraph, and style craft
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop sentence-level style—syntax, rhythm, punctuation, paragraphing—to sustain voice and readability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary sentence length for rhythm; craft paragraphs to control emphasis; avoid pretentious diction; aim for clarity and musicality where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show seeds into fully imagined fiction (imagination over fact)
rubrics_metrics.description: Once you plant seeds from real life, cultivate them with imagination until the story yields maximum entertainment or meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use imagination to sharpen focus and reveal universal truths; fiction can increase rather than reduce 'truth' by selecting and arranging details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid deus ex machina
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not resolve conflicts with implausible or unearned devices that undermine the story's internal logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure resolutions grow from established character choices and plot developments; consequences should feel earned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sensory detail for emotion and thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Convey emotions and interior states through sensory specifics rather than summary statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate feeling into action, bodily sensations, and perceptual detail to make emotional life tangible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline and plotting tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Use outlines, plot graphs, and planning where helpful to organize story structure and pacing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outlines can guide but not straitjacket creativity; use them to ensure progression, tension arcs, and to place scenes effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid clichés and pretentious language
rubrics_metrics.description: Steer clear of stock phrases, tired metaphors, and ostentatious vocabulary that call attention to the writer rather than the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer fresh, precise expression; be suspicious of words used to show off rather than clarify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript formatting and submission basics
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow standard manuscript formatting and know practical submission practices (query letters, slush pile dynamics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adhere to publishers' formatting expectations; craft concise, targeted query letters; understand agents' roles and magazine submission norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: The business of writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn practical aspects: finding agents, publishers, contracts, money, publicity, prepublication, self-publishing, competitions, and awards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study industry practices (agents' roles, contracts, royalties), prepare for prepublication tasks and publicity, and consider both traditional and self-publishing paths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community and career habits
rubrics_metrics.description: Engage with writing groups, classes, conferences, and the larger writing community to develop craft and career.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use feedback, workshops, and networking to grow; balance solitary work with communal learning and professional development.
